clue.text: Music for church service

parts.note: an air is a tune or melody
taken as written
CE stands for Church of England

explanation.surface: Someone choosing the hymns and anthems for a Sunday church service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Music for church service' reads as one phrase about hymns, but 'service' alone is the definition, meaning a branch of the armed forces.
explanation.definitionFit: The armed forces are called the services, and the RAF is one of them.

clue.text: How one's stomach may feel with liver not in order?

indicators.note: putting letters in order means arranging them afresh, so the words liver and not are to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A queasy patient wonders whether a disordered liver explains their churning stomach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not in order' looks like one phrase meaning out of order, but 'not' is part of the letters to shuffle and 'in order?' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A rebelling stomach is a common idiom for nausea, the gut rising up against what was eaten.

clue.text: Acquit, but without costs

explanation.surface: A court clears a defendant and does not make them pay the legal bill.
explanation.definitionFit: To acquit is to release someone from an accusation; something given gratis costs nothing.

clue.text: Raise drink after drink, result — uproar!

indicators.note: after places the rum piece in front of the raised piece

parts.note: rum is a spirit, a drink

indicators.note: in a down entry raising a word lifts it upward, so its letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: to sup is to drink

explanation.surface: A rowdy drinking session: one round after another, ending in a brawl.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'Raise' turns the drink upward, so it reads bottom to top; 'after' puts it behind the spirit, and 'result' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A rumpus is a noisy disturbance or commotion, a synonym of a row.

clue.text: Some rules Pythagoras had to observe

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A geometry pupil learns the rules the Greek mathematician had to follow.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'had to observe' as the definition, but 'had to' cannot stand in for the answer; 'observe' alone is the definition and 'had to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To espy is to catch sight of or notice, so it is a synonym of spot or see.

clue.text: Your pegs are hammered — and these attached

indicators.note: hammered suggests being knocked about out of shape, so the letters of your pegs are rearranged

explanation.surface: A camper drives in tent pegs before tying the lines to them.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the surface: once the pegs are knocked in, these lines are tied to them.
explanation.definitionFit: Guy ropes are tent lines tied to pegs driven into the ground to hold a tent taut.

clue.text: Composer and arranger being oddly selective

indicators.note: selecting oddly means taking only the first, third, fifth and seventh letters of arranger

explanation.surface: A composer and an arranger working together, the arranger fussy and choosy.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Arne was the 18th-century English composer of 'Rule, Britannia!'.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Arne is a well-known English composer, so the name is an example of the category.

clue.text: Stand often taken by public speakers

definitions.text: Stand often taken by public speakers

parts.words: Stand often taken by public speakers
parts.note: both a raised stage that orators stand on and the political position they adopt

explanation.surface: Orators often take a firm stand on the issues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stand' reads as a position or opinion; it is also a raised structure to stand on.
explanation.definitionFit: A platform is a raised stage for speakers, and also a party's declared policy set.

clue.text: Vegetarian, bright-eyed and bushy tailed

parts.note: the idiom for a lively, eager person is taken literally as a description of a nut-eating rodent

explanation.surface: An eager, cheerful person who does not eat meat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bright-eyed and bushy-tailed' is an idiom for alert and keen; here it is a literal description of an animal.
explanation.definitionFit: Squirrels feed on nuts and seeds, have bright eyes and a famously bushy tail.

clue.text: Land set back by a lake

indicators.note: set back means placed in reverse, so the letters of the land are read backwards

parts.note: Eire is the Irish name for Ireland

explanation.surface: A plot of land sits back from the shore of a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: Lake Erie is one of North America's Great Lakes.
explanation.definitionFit: Erie is one of the five Great Lakes, on the US-Canada border.

clue.text: Useless demonstration of hunger-marchers?

parts.note: a pointless protest, and also a march by people whose stomachs have nothing in them

explanation.surface: A march against hunger achieves nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: Hunger-marchers have empty stomachs, so their protest is empty in a second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A futile protest is called hollow or vain, while hungry marchers are literally unfed.

clue.text: Instantly, but not here and now

explanation.surface: A demand for something immediately, though not in the present moment.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means on the spot, immediately; read literally it names a place and a time other than these.

clue.text: Mistakes appear once fuss is made

indicators.note: made here means made up or constructed from scratch, so the letters of once fuss are rebuilt

explanation.surface: Errors come to light once somebody kicks up a fuss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mistakes' looks like a noun but is the verb: to mistake one thing for another.
explanation.definitionFit: To mistake one thing for another is to muddle the two, the same meaning as mixing them up.

clue.text: Post Office workers!

explanation.surface: A slogan about postal workers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Post Office' reads as one name, but it splits: 'Post' and 'Office workers' are the two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: A staff is a pole or stick, like a post; office workers together are the employees of a firm.

clue.text: Quickly put the balance in the Post Office

indicators.note: in tells us the remainder goes inside the Post Office abbreviation

parts.note: PO is the abbreviation for Post Office
the balance is what remains, the rest

explanation.surface: Someone told to hurry and pay the outstanding amount at the post office.
explanation.walkthrough: Presto is the Italian musical direction for a fast tempo.
explanation.definitionFit: In music presto marks a very fast tempo; as an exclamation it means at once.

clue.text: Irritation Ken gets in the kitchen

indicators.note: the answer is what Ken gets put in him to become the kitchen, so taking Ken's letters out of kitchen leaves it

parts.note: taken as written, the man's name

explanation.surface: Ken annoys someone by turning up in their kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: Think of it the other way round: the irritation is what the man's name takes inside it to become the room, so 'gets in the' signals removing his letters from that room.
explanation.definitionFit: An itch is a tickling skin sensation, and by extension any irritation or nagging urge.

clue.text: Takes off meat, it is cooked

indicators.note: cooked suggests being worked over or falsified, so the letters of meat it is are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone removes a joint from the oven, now that it is done.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes off' looks like removing something; it means mimics. 'is' is part of the shuffled letters, not a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To take someone off is to mimic or parody them, the same as copying them.

clue.text: Breaks for a card-game on board

indicators.note: on, as in on board, puts the card game inside the steamship letters

parts.note: SS stands for steamship, and on board means aboard ship
nap is a card game, short for napoleon

explanation.surface: Passengers on a voyage spend their breaks playing cards on deck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On board' is a standard way to put letters inside SS, the steamship.
explanation.definitionFit: To snap is to break suddenly and sharply, so snaps and breaks are synonyms as verbs.

clue.text: Crime publication not for northern readers

parts.note: a southern edition, signalled by S for southern
an edition is one published issue of a paper or book

explanation.surface: A crime paper that is banned in the north.
explanation.walkthrough: A newspaper printed for the south rather than the north is a southern edition, giving S before EDITION.
explanation.definitionFit: Sedition, inciting rebellion against the state, is a criminal offence.

clue.text: Feed a mouse some cheese

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Advice to give a pet mouse a bit of cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: Edam is a mild Dutch variety sold in balls coated with red wax.

clue.text: A word of praise

parts.note: a single word shouted in worship to praise God, from the Hebrew for praise the Lord

explanation.surface: A compliment.
explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a compliment, but the word is literally an expression of praise to God.
explanation.definitionFit: Alleluia is a Hebrew-derived exclamation meaning praise the Lord, used in hymns.

clue.text: It's natural in staple food, we hear

indicators.note: we hear tells us the phrase is spoken, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: bread is the staple food, so this is in bread

explanation.surface: Something is naturally present in bread, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's' is a link; 'natural' is the definition, in the sense of innate.
explanation.definitionFit: An inbred quality is innate or deep-rooted, so natural to someone from birth.

clue.text: Society match?

parts.note: a game played not for points, and the first half of a mutual-aid association's name

explanation.surface: A high-society marriage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Society match' suggests a grand wedding; a friendly is a non-competitive game, and a friendly society is a British mutual insurance body.
explanation.definitionFit: A friendly is a game played for practice, not in a league or cup.

clue.text: I'm about to stay in the same place

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the letters of I'm go round the word for stay

parts.note: taken as written without its apostrophe
to bide is to stay or wait

explanation.surface: Someone announces they are going to stay put.
explanation.walkthrough: Ibidem, usually shortened to ibid., is the Latin used in footnotes for a source already cited.
explanation.definitionFit: Ibidem is Latin for in that very spot, used in citations to repeat a previous reference.

clue.text: The number of the hospital?

parts.note: number read as one who numbs, the person who deadens feeling before surgery

explanation.surface: Asking for the hospital's phone number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' looks like a figure, but read it as 'numb-er', someone who numbs.
explanation.definitionFit: This doctor administers drugs that remove sensation before an operation.

clue.text: Swap services around in church

indicators.note: around in says the answer is found inside the run of letters of the next words

explanation.surface: Churchgoers swapping between services.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a recess at the east end of a church, so 'church' defines it as part for whole.
explanation.definitionFit: An apse is the semicircular recess at the end of a church building.

clue.text: Made to last

parts.note: not built to be durable but stretched out, as scarce supplies are spun out

explanation.surface: Something built to be durable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Made to last' suggests durability; it means stretched out, as in eking out supplies.
explanation.definitionFit: To eke out is to make a small supply go further.

clue.text: The net gain from trawling

parts.note: net read literally as a fishing net, so the catch it brings in

explanation.surface: A boat's profit after costs from fishing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Net gain' suggests profit after expenses; here it is what the net literally gains.
explanation.definitionFit: A haul is the quantity of fish caught in one drag of a net, a catch.

clue.text: Girl embraces chap back in Hamlet's place

indicators.note: embraces means the girl's name wraps round the other piece

parts.note: Elsie is a girl's name

indicators.note: back means the man's name is read in reverse

parts.note: Ron is a man's name

explanation.surface: A girl hugs a man on his return to a small village.
explanation.walkthrough: Elsinore is the castle in Denmark where Shakespeare sets Hamlet; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Hamlet is set at the Danish royal castle at Helsingor, anglicised in the play.

clue.text: Bad comedian was diabolical

indicators.note: bad suggests the comedian's letters are spoiled and rearranged

explanation.surface: A comedian whose act was dreadful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Diabolical' in the surface means dreadful; as the definition it means possessed by a devil.
explanation.definitionFit: Demoniac means relating to or possessed by demons, hence devilish.
